pages.title: What this unit is about
pages.body:
> 💻 **Strand 1 — Introduction To Computing**
Sub-strand 1: Components of Computers and Computer Systems

In Basic 7 you studied fourth-generation computers. Now you will look ahead to the fifth generation, including quantum computers, and meet the direct data entry devices, special printers and flash-based storage that power modern life. You will also manage drives like a technician.

pages.title: Content standard and lessons
pages.body:
> 🎯 **Content standard**
- **B8.1.1.1** Identify parts of a computer and technology tools.
- **B8.1.1.2** Demonstrate the use of the desktop features.

> 🧭 **What you will be able to do**
- **B8.1.1.1.1** Discuss the fifth generation of computers with emphasis on quantum computing.
- **B8.1.1.1.2** Demonstrate understanding of direct data entry devices (graphic tablet, magnetic card reader, optical card reader, QR code reader, RFID readers).
- **B8.1.1.1.3** Examine the uses of the output devices: Braille printers, impact, inkjet, thermal, wax and 3D printers.
- **B8.1.1.1.4** Describe storage devices: flash memory storage systems, embedded flash memory, cards and readers, USB flash drives, SSDs and hybrid hard drives.
- **B8.1.1.2.1** Explore the use of the Charms bar.
- **B8.1.1.2.2** Practise file management techniques (drive management).

> 🗺️ **Lessons in this unit**
- 1.1 The Fifth Generation of Computers and Quantum Computing
- 1.2 Direct Data Entry Devices
- 1.3 Special Output Devices: Printers
- 1.4 Flash Memory and Solid-State Storage
- 1.5 The Charms Bar
- 1.6 Drive Management: Defragmentation, Compression and Partitioning

**Core competencies developed:** Communication and Collaboration (CC8.1), Digital Literacy (DL5.3).

lessons.title: The Fifth Generation of Computers and Quantum Computing

pages.title: The Fifth Generation of Computers and Quantum Computing
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B8.1.1.1.1
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- discuss the features of fifth-generation computers;
- describe quantum computing using Google’s Sycamore processor;
- discuss parallel processing hardware and AI software.
The **fifth generation** of computers is the present and future generation, based on **Artificial Intelligence (AI)**. Its goal is computers that can understand natural language, learn, reason, recognise images and speech, and make decisions. The term became famous through Japan’s **Fifth Generation Computer Systems project (1982–1992)**.
## Features of fifth-generation computers
| **Feature** | **Explanation** |
|---|---|
| Artificial Intelligence software | Programs that learn from data, understand speech and language, recognise faces and objects, and make decisions (e.g. voice assistants, AI chatbots, self-driving systems). |
| Parallel processing hardware | Many processors or cores work on parts of a problem **at the same time**. Modern CPUs have many cores; **GPUs** (graphics processing units) have thousands of small cores and are used to train AI. Supercomputers link thousands of processors together. |
| ULSI and advanced chips | Ultra Large Scale Integration places tens of billions of transistors on one chip. |
| Natural language processing | Computers can talk and listen in human languages. |
| Quantum computing | A new kind of computer that uses the laws of quantum physics (see below). |
| Portability and connectivity | Powerful computing in phones, wearables and the cloud; always connected. |
| Robotics and the Internet of Things | Intelligent machines and everyday objects connected to the Internet. |

pages.title: Quantum computing
pages.body:
## Quantum computing
Ordinary (classical) computers store information as **bits**, each either **0 or 1**. A **quantum computer** uses **quantum bits (qubits)**. Because of a property called **superposition**, a qubit can be in a combination of 0 and 1 at the same time until it is measured. Qubits can also be **entangled**, meaning that the state of one is linked to the state of another. Together, these properties let quantum computers explore a huge number of possibilities at once for certain problems.
[[fig:c8-f02|Figure 1: A classical bit and a qubit]]
**Google’s Sycamore processor**
**Sycamore** is the name of Google’s quantum processor comprising **54 qubits**. In **October 2019**, Google reported that Sycamore, using **53 working qubits** (one qubit on the chip failed), completed a special random-number sampling task in about **200 seconds**. Google estimated that the world’s fastest supercomputer at that time would need about **10,000 years** for the same task, a milestone it called **“quantum supremacy”**. IBM disputed the estimate, arguing that an improved classical method could do it in about 2.5 days. Even so, Sycamore was a historic step.
To work, superconducting qubits like those in Sycamore must be cooled to temperatures colder than outer space (close to **absolute zero, −273 °C**) inside a large refrigerator called a **dilution refrigerator**.

pages.title: Quantum computing (continued)
pages.body:
> ⏳ **Then and now — WHAT YOU WILL SEE TODAY Beyond Sycamore** In **December 2024** Google announced **Willow**, a 105-qubit chip. Willow completed a benchmark computation in under five minutes that Google estimates would take today’s fastest supercomputers 10²⁵ (ten septillion) years, and it showed that errors can be reduced as more qubits are added. IBM, Microsoft, Quantinuum and others are also building quantum computers. Quantum computers are still experimental and are not yet useful for everyday tasks.
| **Possible future uses of quantum computers** | **Why quantum helps** |
|---|---|
| Designing new medicines and materials | Simulating molecules accurately |
| Weather and climate modelling | Handling enormous numbers of variables |
| Optimisation (e.g. traffic, delivery routes, airline schedules) | Testing many combinations efficiently |
| Cryptography | Could break some of today’s encryption, so new “post-quantum” encryption is being developed |
> 🧪 **Activity — Discussion**
In groups, discuss: How might fifth-generation computers change farming, healthcare and education in Ghana over the next 20 years? Present your ideas to the class.

lessons.title: Direct Data Entry Devices

pages.title: Direct Data Entry Devices
Direct Data Entry Devices (continued)
pages.body:
| **Device** | **How it works** | **Real-life uses** |
|---|---|---|
| Graphic tablet (digitiser) | A flat pad on which you draw or write with a special **stylus**; the tablet detects the stylus position and pressure and sends it to the computer. | Digital art and animation, architectural and engineering drawings, signature pads at banks |
| Magnetic card reader | Reads data stored on the **magnetic stripe** on the back of a card when the card is swiped. | Older bank and ATM cards, hotel key cards, ID and loyalty cards (now often replaced by chip cards) |
| Optical card reader (OMR/OCR) | **Optical Mark Recognition (OMR)** detects pencil marks in fixed positions on a form by shining light on it; **OCR** reads printed characters. | Marking multiple-choice answer sheets (e.g. objective tests), lottery slips, surveys, census forms |
| QR code reader | A camera captures the square **Quick Response (QR) code**, and software decodes the pattern into text, a web link, payment details or contact information. | Mobile Money and bank payments, restaurant menus, event tickets, product information, Wi-Fi login |
| RFID reader | Sends radio waves to a **Radio Frequency Identification** tag (a tiny chip and antenna), which replies with its ID number. No line of sight is needed. | Toll booths, contactless bank cards, staff access cards, library books, livestock tracking, e-passports |

pages.title: Direct Data Entry Devices (continued)
pages.body:
[[fig:c8-f03|Figure 2: How an RFID system works]]
> ✨ **Did you know?** The QR code was invented in **1994** by **Masahiro Hara** at the Japanese company **Denso Wave** to track car parts. It can store over 7,000 digits and still be read if part of it is damaged.
## Generating a QR code linked to a website
[[fig:c8-f04|Figure 3: A QR code linking to nacca.gov.gh. Scan it with your phone camera.]]
> 🪜 **Step by step — Creating a QR code for a web page**
1. **Method 1 (Microsoft Edge):** open the web page, e.g. your school’s website. Right-click an empty part of the page and choose **Create QR code for this page** (or click the **Share** icon in the address bar). Click **Download** to save the QR code as a picture.
2. **Method 2 (Google Chrome):** open the page, click the **Share** icon or right-click and choose **Create QR Code**, then **Download**.
3. **Method 3 (online generator):** visit a trusted QR code generator website, paste the web address (URL), choose a colour, and download the image.
4. Insert the QR code image into a Word document or poster and test it with a phone camera before printing.
> 🛡️ **Safety first — QR code scams** Criminals sometimes stick fake QR codes over real ones to send people to fraudulent payment pages. Before paying, check the merchant name that appears on your phone, and never enter your PIN on a website opened from an unknown QR code.

pages.title: Special Output Devices: Printers
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B8.1.1.1.3
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- identify Braille, impact, inkjet, thermal, wax and 3D printers;
- explore their features and how they work in real life.
[[fig:c8-f05|Figure 4: How different printers work]]

pages.title: Special Output Devices: Printers (continued)
pages.body:
| **Printer** | **Features** | **Uses** | **Advantages / disadvantages** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Braille printer (embosser) | Punches raised dots into thick paper to form Braille characters; translation software converts text to Braille | Books, examination papers and notices for blind and visually impaired people | + Gives independence to blind readers; − expensive and noisy; special paper |
| Impact printer (dot matrix, daisy wheel, line printer) | Print head pins strike an inked ribbon against the paper | Invoices and receipts with carbon copies, bank statements, industrial records | + Cheap to run; prints multipart forms; − noisy, slow, low quality |
| Inkjet printer | Sprays tiny droplets of liquid ink through nozzles; colour cartridges or refillable ink tanks | Homes, schools, photo printing | + Cheap to buy; good colour quality; − ink can be expensive; smudges when wet |
| Thermal printer | A heated print head darkens heat-sensitive (thermal) paper, or melts ink from a ribbon (thermal transfer) | Supermarket receipts, POS and Mobile Money agent receipts, ATM slips, barcode labels, tickets | + Quiet, fast, no ink needed; − thermal print fades over time and with heat |
| Wax (solid ink / thermal wax) printer | Heat melts coloured wax from a ribbon or solid ink sticks onto the paper, giving bright, sharp colours | Colour labels, signs, proofs for graphic design | + Vivid colours on many surfaces; − slow warm-up, less common today |
| 3D printer | Builds a solid object layer by layer from melted plastic filament (FDM) or liquid resin cured by light (SLA), following a 3D computer model | Prototypes, spare parts, prosthetic limbs, school models, dental and medical models, even houses | + Makes complex shapes cheaply; − slow; limited materials and size |

pages.title: Special Output Devices: Printers (continued)
pages.body:
> 🇬🇭 **Ghana connection** Schools for the blind in Ghana, such as the **Akropong School for the Blind** and the **Wa School for the Blind**, use Braille embossers and Braille writers so that learners can read textbooks and write examinations.
> 🧪 **Activity — Printer hunt**
Collect samples: a supermarket or Mobile Money receipt (thermal), a page from an inkjet printer, and a dot-matrix invoice if possible. Compare their quality. Leave the thermal receipt in the sun for a day and observe what happens.

lessons.title: Flash Memory and Solid-State Storage

pages.title: Flash Memory and Solid-State Storage
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B8.1.1.1.4
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- describe flash memory storage systems;
- describe embedded flash memory, memory cards and readers, USB flash drives, SSDs and hybrid drives;
- illustrate their uses.
**Flash memory** is a type of **non-volatile** memory chip: it keeps data without power and has **no moving parts**. Data is stored as electrical charges in memory cells (NAND flash). Flash memory is fast, light, silent and resistant to knocks, which makes it ideal for portable devices.
| **Storage device** | **Description** | **Typical capacity (2026)** | **Uses** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Embedded flash memory | Flash chips built permanently into a device’s circuit board (eMMC, UFS) | 32 GB – 1 TB | Smartphones, tablets, smart TVs, cameras, cars |
| Flash memory cards | Small removable cards: **SD**, **microSD**, CompactFlash. Classes: SDHC (up to 32 GB), SDXC (up to 2 TB) | 16 GB – 1 TB+ | Cameras, phones, drones, game consoles |
| Card readers | Devices or slots that let a computer read memory cards (built-in slot or USB adapter) | — | Transferring photos from a camera to a computer |
| USB flash drive (pen drive) | Flash memory with a USB plug; plug-and-play | 16 GB – 1 TB | Carrying school files, backups, installing software |
| Solid State Drive (SSD) | A drive made of flash chips that replaces a hard disk. **SATA SSDs** (≈550 MB/s) and much faster **NVMe M.2 SSDs** (3,000–7,000+ MB/s) | 256 GB – 8 TB | Laptops and desktops: very fast start-up and loading |
| Hybrid hard drive (SSHD) | A normal hard disk combined with a small amount of flash memory that caches the most-used files | 1 TB – 4 TB | Budget computers that need large capacity with some speed boost |

pages.title: Flash Memory and Solid-State Storage (continued)
pages.body:
[[fig:c8-f06|Figure 5: Typical read speeds of storage devices]]
| **SSD compared with HDD** | **SSD** | **HDD** |
|---|---|---|
| Moving parts | None | Spinning platters and moving heads |
| Speed | Much faster | Slower |
| Noise and heat | Silent, cool | Some noise and heat |
| Shock resistance | High | Can be damaged if dropped while running |
| Cost per GB | Higher | Lower |
| Capacity for the price | Smaller | Larger |
> 🛡️ **Safety first — Protect your flash storage** Always use **Safely Remove Hardware / Eject** before unplugging a USB drive or memory card; scan flash drives for viruses before opening files; and keep a backup copy, because flash drives are easily lost.

pages.title: The Charms Bar
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B8.1.1.2.1
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- identify the icons in the Charms bar;
- describe the features of each charm;
- find the equivalent features in Windows 10 and 11.
The **Charms bar** was a vertical bar of five buttons (charms) introduced in **Windows 8 and 8.1**. It appeared on the right side of the screen when you pointed the mouse to the top-right or bottom-right corner, swiped in from the right edge of a touchscreen, or pressed **Windows key + C**.
[[fig:c8-f07|Figure 6: The Windows 8 Start screen with the Charms bar]]
| **Charm** | **Function in Windows 8** | **Equivalent in Windows 10 / 11** |
|---|---|---|
| Search | Search for apps, files, settings and the web | Search box/icon on the taskbar, or **Windows + S** |
| Share | Share content from the current app (e.g. email a photo) | **Share** button in apps and File Explorer; **Nearby sharing** |
| Start | Go to the Start screen | **Start** button or **Windows key** |
| Devices | Send content to printers, projectors and other devices | **Settings › Bluetooth & devices**; **Windows + P** (project); **Windows + K** (cast) |
| Settings | Settings for the current app, plus volume, brightness, network, power | **Settings app (Windows + I)**; **Quick Settings (Windows + A)** for Wi-Fi, volume and brightness |

pages.title: The Charms Bar (continued)
pages.body: > ⏳ **Then and now — WHAT YOU WILL SEE TODAY** Microsoft removed the Charms bar in **Windows 10 (2015)**. You may still find Windows 8.1 on some older school computers, but its support ended in January 2023. Knowing the charms helps you understand where these features moved.

lessons.title: Drive Management: Defragmentation, Compression and Partitioning

pages.title: Drive Management: Defragmentation, Compression and Partitioning
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B8.1.1.2.2
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- explain and perform defragmentation;
- compress and extract files;
- explore ways of partitioning a hard disk.
## Defragmentation
When files are saved, changed and deleted, a hard disk stores parts of a file in different places. This is called **fragmentation**, and it slows the drive down because the read/write head must jump around. **Defragmentation** rearranges the pieces so that each file is stored in one continuous area.
[[fig:c8-f08|Figure 7: A disk before and after defragmentation]]
> 🪜 **Step by step — Optimising a drive in Windows**
1. Click **Start**, type defrag and open **Defragment and Optimise Drives**.
2. Select the drive, e.g. **(C:)**, and click **Analyse** to see the percentage fragmented.
3. Click **Optimise**. Windows defragments hard disks; for SSDs it sends a **TRIM** command instead.
4. Under **Scheduled optimisation**, make sure it is set to run **Weekly**.
> 🎯 **BECE focus** **SSDs should not be defragmented** in the traditional way. They have no moving heads, so fragmentation does not slow them, and unnecessary writing shortens their life. Windows handles this automatically.
## File compression
**Compression** reduces the size of files so they take up less storage and are faster to send by email or WhatsApp. A **ZIP** file can hold many files and folders in one compressed file. Text and documents compress well; photos (.jpg) and videos (.mp4) are already compressed and shrink little.

pages.title: Drive Management: Defragmentation, Compression and Partitioning (continued)
pages.body:
> 🪜 **Step by step — Compressing and extracting files**
1. In File Explorer, select the files or folder to compress.
2. Right-click › **Compress to ZIP file** (Windows 11) or **Send to › Compressed (zipped) folder** (Windows 10).
3. A new .zip file appears; type a name and press **Enter**.
4. To **extract**, right-click the ZIP file › **Extract All…**, choose a destination and click **Extract**.
## Partitioning a hard disk
A **partition** is a section of a physical disk that Windows treats as a separate drive with its own letter (C:, D:). Partitioning lets you separate the operating system from personal data, install two operating systems (dual-boot), or organise storage.
[[fig:c8-f09|Figure 8: A disk divided into partitions]]
> 🪜 **Step by step — Exploring partitions with Disk Management (teacher demonstration)**
1. Right-click **Start** and choose **Disk Management** (or run diskmgmt.msc).
2. Observe each disk, its partitions, drive letters, file system (NTFS) and free space.
3. To create a partition from free space: right-click a volume with space › **Shrink Volume**, enter the amount, then right-click the **Unallocated** space › **New Simple Volume** and follow the wizard (size, drive letter, format as NTFS).
> 🛡️ **Safety first** Partitioning and formatting can **erase all data**. Always back up first, and practise only on a spare disk under your teacher’s supervision.

pages.title: Review: written and practical tasks
pages.body:
> ✏️ **Review exercises** — answer these in your exercise book or on the computer, then check with your teacher.
## Short answer questions
1. State **four** features of fifth-generation computers.
2. Describe Google’s Sycamore quantum processor and its 2019 achievement.
3. Explain how an RFID system works and give **three** uses.
4. Compare inkjet and thermal printers.
5. Give **three** advantages of SSDs over HDDs.
6. List the five charms and their Windows 11 equivalents.
7. Why should an SSD not be defragmented?
## Practical tasks
1. Generate a QR code linking to your school’s (or the NaCCA) website and insert it into a Word document.
2. Compress a folder of your class notes into a ZIP file. Compare the original and compressed sizes.
